faq.a: Pangaea was a supercontinent that joined almost all the land on Earth, from about 335 to 200 million years ago. Its name means all lands.

faq.q: How do we know the continents moved?
faq.a: The coasts of South America and Africa fit like jigsaw pieces, matching fossils and rocks are found on both sides of oceans, and today satellites measure the plates moving each year.
asks: What is the evidence for continental drift?

faq.a: Probably. Because the plates keep moving, scientists predict a new supercontinent in roughly 200 to 300 million years, though they are not sure exactly how it will form.
asks: What will the Earth look like in the future?

faq.a: The German scientist Alfred Wegener proposed in 1912 that continents drift. Many people doubted him because he could not explain how. Plate tectonics explained it in the 1960s.
No. Earth has probably had several supercontinents that formed and broke apart over billions of years, such as Rodinia about a billion years ago.

facts: Pangaea began to break apart about 200 million years ago.
Alfred Wegener proposed the idea of continental drift in 1912.
The Atlantic Ocean is widening by about 2 to 5 centimetres a year.
